The macOS root bug

su root

On 28 November 2017 I asked Apple Support, on Twitter, whether it knew that anyone could log in as “root” on macOS High Sierra with an empty password. Within hours tech news sites had picked it up, by the next day it was in newspapers from the United States to China, and that same day Apple shipped a fix and apologised. This is the story as I told it then, and what I learned from it.

Bug

Affected
macOS High Sierra 10.13 and 10.13.1[2]
Severity
8.1 of 10, High (CVSS 3.0)[1]
The tweet
28 November 2017, 21:38 in Istanbul[3]
Fixed
Security Update 2017-001, 29 November 2017[2]
Noticed by
The infrastructure team of the company I worked for, not me; it had been on Apple's forums since 13 November[4]

The tweet

Nine minutes later I posted the steps: open System Preferences, go to Users & Groups and click the lock to make changes, then type “root” with no password, and try it several times. “Result is unbelievable!”[5]

How we noticed it

I am not the one who discovered the bug, and I wrote so the day after the tweet.[4] About a week before it, the infrastructure staff at the company I worked for stumbled on the issue while helping one of my colleagues get back into his local admin account, and they used the flaw to recover it. On 23 November they reported it to Apple. Searching online, they found it already mentioned in a few places, even on Apple's Developer Forums on 13 November. The issue had been revealed, but Apple had not noticed yet.[4]

On 28 November the staff told me they had to set a root password on my Mac so that it would not be open to it. I saw the issue with my own eyes and could not believe it.[4] “They tried the same thing at my machine and worked. It scared us a lot,” I told Motherboard that night.[6] The issue was serious, it had already been mentioned in public forums weeks before, and I thought I had to ask Apple whether it was aware of it. So I asked on Twitter.[4]

I am neither a hacker nor a security specialist. I had no intention to harm Apple or its users; I wanted to warn Apple that there was a serious security issue in High Sierra, so that it would fix it.[4]

Apple's answer

Apple Support replied to my tweet that evening and asked me to send a direct message with my Mac model and macOS version.[7] The same night Apple told the press it was working on a software update, and that setting a root password would block unauthorised access until then.[8]

The next day, 29 November, Apple released Security Update 2017-001. Its notes describe the flaw in one sentence: “A logic error existed in the validation of credentials. This was addressed with improved credential validation.”[2] On a Mac upgraded from 10.13 to 10.13.1 the fix needed a reboot, or the bug came back.[2][10] Apple also apologised:

Going public

The criticism came as fast as the coverage. I should have told Apple privately, the argument went, and given it time to patch the bug before anyone heard of it.[7][11]

Four months later I took that argument on stage at Women Techmakers Istanbul, in a talk called “Irresponsible Disclosure: Short Handbook of an Ethical Developer”.[12] The rule I give there is the one my critics gave: it does not matter whether a company runs a bug bounty program; report a vulnerability to it privately, through private channels, and keep it confidential. Then comes the turn: we had already done exactly that. Our infrastructure team had contacted Apple several times. One of those messages went out on 23 November, five days before the tweet, and ended: “I don't think you can resolve this issue, therefore I want to talk with someone from security.”[12]

By then a private report was no longer enough. The flaw had been public for two weeks, which meant it could already be on the deep web, and attackers could already be using it to get into machines as root.[12]

The talk puts this inside a longer list, the principles of an ethical developer. On security it reads: we apply secure coding practices, we test the security of our software, we do not keep passwords in clear text, we remove passwords from external files, we protect log files and all internals, and we inform about security vulnerabilities. On social media: we show respect.[12]

In the press

grep -ri lemi

The story ran in tech news sites and newspapers around the world, and many of them told it with two errors. They wrote that I discovered the bug, and that nobody had told Apple before the tweet. Our staff noticed it, and reported it to Apple five days before I tweeted.[4][12] Apple's own statement said its security engineers became aware of the issue on Tuesday afternoon, the day of the tweet.[9] My name came out in a few new spellings too: Lemi Ergin, Lemi Orhan Ergan, Lemi Orhan Engin and Erign.[7][13][14][10]

Each article below names me or embeds my tweet. Ars Technica and Wired covered the bug as well; both are among the references of its CVE entry.[1]
